diagram.caption: Genetic drift in simulated populations

stem: Which of the following processes changes allele frequencies in a population in a nonrandom way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bottleneck effect, because the survivors of an event are always the individuals with the alleles that are best for the environment
choices.explanation: In a bottleneck, the survivors are a chance sample.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mutation, because the environment determines which alleles will be produced by a mutation in the DNA of the individuals
choices.explanation: Mutation is random and is not directed by the environment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Natural selection, because individuals with certain phenotypes survive and reproduce more often than the others in the environment
choices.explanation: Natural selection is nonrandom with respect to fitness. Drift and mutation are random.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genetic drift, because the alleles of the individuals who survive in a small population are chosen by their fitness in the environment
choices.explanation: Genetic drift is a random process and does not depend on fitness.

explanation: Natural selection is nonrandom; mutation, drift and the founder and bottleneck effects are random.

stem: A population of 200 animals has a frequency of 0.50 for an allele. 50 migrants with a frequency of 0.10 for the same allele join the population and breed with the residents. What is the new frequency of the allele in the combined population?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.30, because the new frequency is the simple average of the two frequencies, regardless of the sizes of the groups.
choices.explanation: The groups have different sizes, so the frequencies are weighted by the numbers of animals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.42, because the allele copies from all 250 animals are averaged: (200 x 0.50 + 50 x 0.10) / 250.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.50, because the frequency of an allele in a population cannot be changed by the arrival of animals from outside.
choices.explanation: Migration can change allele frequencies by adding or removing alleles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.40, because the migrants remove their allele frequency from that of the residents in the combined population.
choices.explanation: The migrants add their alleles to the population. They do not subtract them.

explanation: Gene flow changes allele frequencies by adding alleles from the migrants.

stem: The table shows the frequencies of two alleles in a population in three consecutive generations. Which statement is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evolution has not occurred in the population, because the sum of the frequencies of the two alleles is 1.00 in each generation.
choices.explanation: The sum is always 1. Evolution is shown by a change in the individual frequencies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evolution has occurred only in the first generation, because evolution requires a change in the number of individuals.
choices.explanation: Evolution is defined by changes in allele frequencies, not in the number of individuals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evolution has occurred in the population only if the frequency of allele A fell by more than half during the three generations.
choices.explanation: Any change in allele frequencies over generations is evolution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evolution has occurred in the population, because the frequencies of the alleles changed from one generation to the next.
choices.explanation: Changes in allele frequencies provide evidence for the occurrence of evolution in a population.

explanation: Changes in allele frequencies over generations are evidence of evolution.

stem: Two populations of the same species live on different sides of a river. Occasionally some individuals swim across the river and breed in the other population. Which prediction is most consistent with this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The populations are certain to become two species, because the river is a physical barrier that stops all of the mating between them.
choices.explanation: The river does not stop all gene flow, and gene flow prevents divergence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The populations are more likely to diverge into separate species, because the individuals that swim are the fittest individuals in each population.
choices.explanation: The exchange of alleles makes the populations more alike.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The populations will each lose all of their genetic variation, because migrating individuals cannot carry any alleles with them.
choices.explanation: Migrants carry alleles, and gene flow can add to the variation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The populations are less likely to diverge into separate species, because the movement of individuals exchanges alleles between them.
choices.explanation: Gene flow between two populations prevents them from diverging into separate species.

explanation: Gene flow keeps populations from diverging.

stem: Which of the following is a condition that must be met for a population to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mating in the population is random with respect to the gene, and the population is large enough that genetic drift is negligible.
choices.explanation: Conditions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: a large population, no migration, no new mutations, random mating and no natural selection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Individuals with certain genotypes survive and reproduce more than the others, so that selection keeps the allele frequencies steady.
choices.explanation: Natural selection is not allowed in a population in equilibrium.

choices.label: C
choices.text: New mutations occur at a high rate in the population, so that the variation in the alleles is renewed in every generation.
choices.explanation: There must be no new mutations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Individuals move into and out of the population freely, so that new alleles are added to the gene pool in every generation.
choices.explanation: There must be no migration.

explanation: Hardy-Weinberg conditions: large population, no migration, no new mutations, random mating, no natural selection.

stem: In the Hardy-Weinberg equation, $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$, what does the term $2pq$ represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The frequency of the heterozygous individuals in the whole population, which have one copy of each of the two alleles
choices.explanation: In the equation, 2pq is the frequency of heterozygotes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The frequency of homozygous recessive individuals in the population, which have two copies of the recessive allele
choices.explanation: The frequency of homozygous recessive individuals is q squared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The frequency of the dominant allele in the population, which is found in the homozygous dominant individuals only
choices.explanation: The frequency of an allele is p or q, not 2pq.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The frequency of all of the alleles in the population, which is the sum of the dominant and the recessive alleles
choices.explanation: The sum of the frequencies of the alleles is p + q = 1.

explanation: p squared and q squared are the homozygotes; 2pq is the heterozygotes.

stem: In a population that is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of homozygous recessive individuals ($q^2$) is 0.04. What is the frequency of heterozygous individuals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.96, because all of the individuals that are not homozygous recessive are heterozygous in the population.
choices.explanation: Individuals that are not homozygous recessive include the homozygous dominant ones.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.20, because the square root of 0.04 is the frequency of heterozygous individuals in the population.
choices.explanation: 0.20 is the frequency of the recessive allele (q), not the frequency of heterozygotes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: q = the square root of 0.04 = 0.2, p = 0.8, and 2pq = 0.32.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.64, because that is the frequency of the homozygous dominant individuals when p is 0.8 in the population.
choices.explanation: p squared is the frequency of the homozygous dominant individuals, not of the heterozygotes.

explanation: q squared gives q; then p = 1 - q and the heterozygotes are 2pq.

stem: In a population of 1,000 individuals that is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 360 individuals have the recessive phenotype for a trait. About how many individuals are heterozygous for the trait?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: q squared = 360 / 1,000 = 0.36, so q = 0.6, p = 0.4, and 2pq = 0.48, which is 480 individuals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 160, because the individuals that are not homozygous recessive are all heterozygous in the population.
choices.explanation: That is the number of homozygous dominant individuals (p squared x N).

choices.label: C
choices.text: 600, because the frequency of the recessive allele is the frequency of the heterozygous individuals.
choices.explanation: q is the frequency of the recessive allele and not of the heterozygous individuals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 360, because the number of individuals with the recessive phenotype is also the number that are heterozygous.
choices.explanation: The recessive phenotype is shown by the homozygous recessive individuals only. The heterozygotes are another group.

explanation: q squared = frequency of the recessive phenotype; then 2pq gives the heterozygotes.

stem: A population of 100 individuals has 50 with the genotype AA, 40 with the genotype Aa, and 10 with the genotype aa. What is the frequency of the allele A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.90, because the allele is present in the individuals that have the AA and the Aa genotypes.
choices.explanation: This counts individuals and not alleles, and the Aa individuals have only one copy of A.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1.40, because the number of copies of A is divided by the number of individuals.
choices.explanation: The number of copies must be divided by the number of alleles, which is twice the number of individuals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.70, because there are 140 copies of A among the 200 alleles in the population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.50, because the frequency of the allele is the same as the frequency of the AA genotype.
choices.explanation: Heterozygotes also carry one copy of A.

explanation: Allele frequency = copies of the allele / total alleles (2N for a diploid).

stem: The allele frequencies in a population are p = 0.7 and q = 0.3. The table shows the genotype frequencies expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and the frequencies that were observed. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The population is not in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, so one or more of the conditions are not met, for example if mating is not random.
choices.explanation: The observed frequencies differ greatly from the expected ones, so at least one condition for equilibrium is not met.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, because the observed frequency of the genotype AA is higher than 0.49.
choices.explanation: A difference from the expected value shows that the population is not in equilibrium.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The allele frequencies must be wrong, because the observed frequencies of the genotypes cannot differ from the expected ones.
choices.explanation: The observed genotype frequencies can differ from the expected ones when conditions are not met.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, because the observed frequencies add up to 1.00 and so they match the expected values.
choices.explanation: The sum is always 1. What matters is whether each frequency matches the expected value.

explanation: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a null hypothesis; large deviations show that a condition is not met.

stem: No real population meets all of the conditions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Why is the model still useful to biologists?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that real populations never change, so a biologist can use it to predict the allele frequencies of a population in the future.
choices.explanation: The model describes a non-evolving population, and real populations do change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It proves that natural selection is the only process that changes allele frequencies, so the other processes can be ignored.
choices.explanation: Drift, gene flow and mutation also change allele frequencies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It provides a null hypothesis for a non-evolving population, so a difference from the predicted frequencies suggests that evolution is occurring.
choices.explanation: The conditions are never met, but they provide a valuable null hypothesis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It gives the exact genotype frequencies of every real population, so a biologist does not need to count the individuals.
choices.explanation: The model predicts frequencies for an ideal population. Real populations must be sampled.

explanation: The Hardy-Weinberg model is a null hypothesis for a non-evolving population.

stem: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 2,500 people in a population that is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. About what fraction of the people are carriers (heterozygotes)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 0.0004, or about 1 in 2,500, because the carriers are as common as the people who are affected by the disorder.
choices.explanation: 0.0004 is q squared, the frequency of the affected people. Carriers are much more common.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 0.96, or about 24 in 25, because most of the people in the population are carriers of the disorder.
choices.explanation: 0.96 is the frequency of the homozygous dominant people, who are not carriers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 0.02, or about 1 in 50, because the frequency of carriers is the same as the frequency of the recessive allele.
choices.explanation: 0.02 is the frequency of the allele (q). Carriers have a frequency of 2pq.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 0.039, or about 1 in 26, because q = 0.02, p = 0.98, and 2pq = 0.039.

explanation: Carriers (2pq) are much more common than affected people (q squared) for a rare recessive allele.

stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of an allele a is 0.50. All of the individuals with the genotype aa die before they reproduce, and the survivors mate at random. What is the frequency of the allele a among the gametes of the survivors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.00, because the allele a is removed from the population when all of the individuals with the genotype aa die.
choices.explanation: The heterozygotes still carry the allele a.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.50, because the frequency of an allele in a population does not change when individuals die before they reproduce.
choices.explanation: Selection against a genotype changes allele frequencies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.25, because the individuals with the genotype aa were 25% of the population, and they are the only source of the allele.
choices.explanation: The allele is also carried by the heterozygotes, which survive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 0.33, because the survivors are 25% AA and 50% Aa, and a is carried by half of the alleles of the Aa individuals.
choices.explanation: The survivors are 0.25 AA and 0.50 Aa, so a = (0.50 / 2) / 0.75 = 0.33.

explanation: Selection against a genotype changes allele frequencies, so the population is no longer in equilibrium.

stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of the dominant allele (p) is 0.6. What is the expected frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype in the next generation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.48, because the frequency of the genotype is calculated as two times p times q for the population.
choices.explanation: 2pq is the frequency of heterozygotes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.36, because the frequency of the genotype is p squared and 0.6 x 0.6 = 0.36.
choices.explanation: The frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype is p squared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.60, because the frequency of the genotype is the same as the frequency of the allele in the population.
choices.explanation: The genotype needs two copies of the allele, so its frequency is p squared.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.16, because the frequency of the genotype is the square of the frequency of the other allele.
choices.explanation: q squared is the frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype.

explanation: The frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype is p squared.

stem: Which of the following is an example of biochemical evidence for evolution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bones in the forelimbs of a bat, a whale and a human have the same arrangement, though they are used in different ways.
choices.explanation: This is morphological (anatomical) evidence and not biochemical evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The species on a chain of islands are more similar to the species on the nearest mainland than to species on other continents.
choices.explanation: This is geographical evidence from the distribution of species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fossils of simple organisms are found in older layers of rock and the fossils of complex organisms are found in younger layers of rock.
choices.explanation: This is geological evidence from the fossil record.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sequence of amino acids in a protein is very similar in two species, and it differs more in a species that is less closely related.
choices.explanation: A comparison of DNA nucleotide sequences and protein amino acid sequences provides evidence for evolution and common ancestry.

explanation: Evolution is supported by geographical, geological, physical, biochemical and mathematical data.

stem: Which of the following can be used to determine the age of a fossil?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The age of the layer of rock in which the fossil is found, and the rate of decay of radioactive isotopes such as carbon-14
choices.explanation: Fossils can be dated by the age of the rocks and by the rate of decay of isotopes including carbon-14.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The size of the fossil compared with a living relative, and the number of genes that the living relative has in its genome
choices.explanation: The size of a fossil does not give its age, and a fossil usually has no intact genome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number of species that are alive today and that look similar to the fossil, and the habitat that those species now live in
choices.explanation: Living species do not determine the age of a fossil.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pH of the water that was used to clean the fossil in the laboratory, and the length of time that the fossil was stored
choices.explanation: The treatment of a fossil in the laboratory does not give its age.

explanation: Fossils are dated by the age of the rocks, isotope decay and geographical data.

stem: The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years. A wooden tool is found to have 25% of the carbon-14 that a living tree has. About how old is the tool?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 4,297 years, because the tool has lost 75% of its carbon-14 and so 75% of one half-life has passed.
choices.explanation: Decay is exponential, not linear. Losing 75% takes two half-lives.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5,730 years, because the amount of carbon-14 falls to 25% during the first half-life of the isotope.
choices.explanation: After one half-life, 50% remains. 25% remains after two half-lives.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 22,920 years, because the amount of carbon-14 falls by 25% in each of the half-lives of the isotope.
choices.explanation: The amount of the isotope halves in each half-life, and it does not fall by 25%.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 11,460 years, because 25% is what remains after two half-lives of 5,730 years each.
choices.explanation: 1 / 2 x 1 / 2 = 1 / 4, so two half-lives have passed: 2 x 5,730 = 11,460.

explanation: After n half-lives, (1/2)^n of the isotope remains.

stem: The forelimbs of humans, bats and whales have the same arrangement of bones, though the limbs are used for grasping, flying and swimming. Which statement best explains this similarity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The three species have the same arrangement of bones by chance, because the bones form in a random order in the embryo of each species.
choices.explanation: The shared pattern is too detailed to be explained by chance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The three species acquired the same arrangement of bones during their lives, because they all use their forelimbs often and in similar ways.
choices.explanation: The limbs are used in different ways, and acquired changes are not inherited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The three species each evolved the same arrangement of bones separately, because the arrangement is the best design for any kind of forelimb.
choices.explanation: The different uses of the limbs show that the shared arrangement is not the best design for all uses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The three species descended from a common ancestor that had this arrangement of bones, which has been modified in each lineage.
choices.explanation: Morphological homologies provide evidence of common ancestry.

explanation: Homologous structures are evidence of common ancestry.

stem: Whales have small pelvic bones that are not attached to the backbone and that have no function in swimming. Which statement is best supported by this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whales developed the pelvic bones during their lives, because the animals use the bones more as they grow older and larger.
choices.explanation: The bones are not used, and acquired characteristics are not inherited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whales descended from ancestors with hind limbs, and the structure is a vestigial remnant that provides evidence of common ancestry.
choices.explanation: Vestigial structures are morphological homologies that provide evidence of common ancestry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whales are not related to any land animals, because the pelvic bones of whales do not have any function in the animals.
choices.explanation: A vestigial structure supports a relationship with land animals that have functional pelvic bones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whales will evolve hind limbs in the next generations, because the bones show that the whales need them in order to survive.
choices.explanation: Evolution does not occur in response to needs, and vestigial structures are leftovers.

explanation: Vestigial structures are evidence of common ancestry.

stem: The table shows the number of differences in the amino acid sequence of a protein of 140 amino acids between a human and three other species. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Species 3 is the most closely related to humans of the three, because its protein sequence has the most differences from the human sequence.
choices.explanation: More differences suggest a more distant relationship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Species 2 is the most closely related to humans of the three, because its protein sequence differs from the human sequence by an intermediate amount.
choices.explanation: The species with the fewest differences is the most closely related.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The three species are equally related to humans, because all of them have the same protein with the same number of amino acids.
choices.explanation: The numbers of differences are not the same, which shows different degrees of relatedness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Species 1 is the most closely related to humans of the three, because its protein sequence has the fewest differences from the human sequence.
choices.explanation: A comparison of protein sequences provides evidence for relationships. Fewer differences suggest a more recent common ancestor.

explanation: Fewer sequence differences suggest a more recent common ancestor.

diagram.caption: Differences in a protein of 140 amino acids

stem: Differences in a protein sequence accumulate at a constant rate. Two species whose lineages separated 24 million years ago differ at 12 amino acids. Two other species differ at 30 amino acids. About how long ago did the lineages of the other two species separate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 10 million years ago, because the greater the number of differences, the shorter the time since the lineages separated.
choices.explanation: More differences mean more time has passed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 60 million years ago, because the rate is 0.5 difference per million years and 30 / 0.5 = 60.
choices.explanation: The rate is 12 / 24 = 0.5 differences per million years, so 30 differences take 60 million years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 42 million years ago, because the extra 18 differences are added to the 24 million years of the first pair.
choices.explanation: The time is found from the rate of change, and not by adding the differences to the years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 15 million years ago, because the number of differences is multiplied by the rate of 0.5 per million years.
choices.explanation: The number of differences must be divided by the rate to give the time.

explanation: A molecular clock: time = differences / rate.

stem: In a series of undisturbed rock layers, fossils of simple, single-celled organisms are found in the deepest layers, and fossils of more complex organisms appear in higher layers. Which statement is best supported by this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All of the species lived at the same time, because the fossils of the simple and the complex organisms are found in the same rock sequence.
choices.explanation: The layers have different ages, and the fossils in them are of different ages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Life on Earth has changed over time, because the oldest layers are deeper, and different organisms are found in layers of different ages.
choices.explanation: Geological data show that organisms have changed over time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: New layers of rock form from the fossils, because the organisms in the higher layers made the rock from their own bodies.
choices.explanation: Layers form by deposition of sediments, and fossils are found in them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The complex organisms changed into the simple organisms, because the simple organisms are found in the deeper layers of the rock.
choices.explanation: The deeper (older) layers contain the simple organisms, so the order is the opposite.

explanation: The fossil record in layers of rock shows change over time.

stem: Two lizard species on separate continents have a similar body shape but are not closely related, according to DNA data. A student claims that the similar body shape shows that the two species have a recent common ancestor. How should the student's claim be evaluated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim is not well supported, because molecular data are usually more reliable than morphology, and similar shapes can evolve separately.
choices.explanation: Molecular data typically provide more accurate and reliable evidence than morphological traits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is well supported, because two species with a similar body shape must have gotten it from a recent common ancestor.
choices.explanation: Similar traits can evolve separately in response to similar selective pressures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim is well supported, because the body shape of an organism is always more reliable evidence than its DNA sequence.
choices.explanation: DNA data are typically more reliable than body shape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim cannot be evaluated, because the DNA of a species does not contain information about its evolutionary history.
choices.explanation: DNA sequences are used to infer evolutionary relationships.

explanation: Molecular data are typically more reliable than morphology for inferring relationships.

stem: Which set of features is shared by all eukaryotes and provides evidence of their common ancestry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A circular chromosome, ribosomes, and genes that are grouped in operons that are transcribed together
choices.explanation: These are features of prokaryotes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A plasma membrane, ribosomes, and DNA as the genetic material of the cell in all of the cell types
choices.explanation: These are found in all cells, including prokaryotes, and so they do not separate eukaryotes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Membrane-bound organelles, linear chromosomes, and genes that contain introns
choices.explanation: Structural and functional evidence of the common ancestry of all eukaryotes includes these three features.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A cell wall, chloroplasts, and the ability to carry out photosynthesis in the light from the sun
choices.explanation: These are not found in all eukaryotes. Animals lack all three.

explanation: Shared features of eukaryotes: membrane-bound organelles, linear chromosomes, genes with introns.

stem: Genes that contain introns are found in plants, fungi and animals. Which statement best explains why this observation supports a common ancestry of eukaryotes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Introns are needed for all organisms to survive, and so every organism has to have genes with introns in order to live.
choices.explanation: Prokaryotes lack introns and survive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Introns are found in the genes of prokaryotes and eukaryotes alike, and so all of the organisms on Earth have a common ancestor.
choices.explanation: Introns are typical of eukaryotic genes and not of prokaryotes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Introns are produced by the environment in each organism, and so organisms in the same environment will have introns.
choices.explanation: Introns are part of the genes and are inherited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is unlikely that such a complex feature evolved separately in each lineage, and so it was probably present in a common ancestor of the eukaryotes.
choices.explanation: Shared complex features suggest inheritance from a common ancestor.

explanation: Genes with introns are shared by eukaryotes, evidence of common ancestry.

stem: Scientists discover a single-celled organism in a lake. It has a nucleus, several linear chromosomes, and genes that contain introns. Which prediction about the organism is best supported by these features?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a virus, because viruses have only a few genes and can be found in water in the lakes of all regions.
choices.explanation: A virus is not a cell and does not have a nucleus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a eukaryote, and it shares a common ancestor with other eukaryotes such as plants, fungi and animals.
choices.explanation: Linear chromosomes and genes with introns are features of eukaryotes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cannot be classified, because the features of cells do not show how an organism is related to the other organisms.
choices.explanation: Structural features are used to infer relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a prokaryote, because most of the single-celled organisms in lakes are prokaryotes and they have a nucleus.
choices.explanation: Prokaryotes do not have a nucleus, linear chromosomes or introns.

explanation: Linear chromosomes and introns are shared eukaryotic features.

stem: The table shows three features of four organisms. Which statement is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All four organisms are eukaryotes, because every organism has a membrane and takes in energy from its environment.
choices.explanation: Two of the organisms lack the three features that are shared by eukaryotes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Organisms X and Z share the features of eukaryotes, which suggests that they share a common ancestor that was a eukaryote.
choices.explanation: Organisms X and Z lack the three features, so they are probably prokaryotes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Organisms W and X share the features of eukaryotes, which suggests that they share a common ancestor that was a eukaryote.
choices.explanation: Organism X lacks all three features.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Organisms W and Y share the features of eukaryotes, which suggests that they share a common ancestor that was a eukaryote.
choices.explanation: Membrane-bound organelles, linear chromosomes and introns are features of eukaryotes.

explanation: Shared features of eukaryotes suggest a shared ancestor.

stem: If all eukaryotes descended from a common ancestor, which observation would be expected in the cells of a newly discovered eukaryote?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cells have no membrane-bound organelles, and the DNA is organized into a single circular chromosome.
choices.explanation: These are features of prokaryotes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cells have chloroplasts and cell walls, and they carry out photosynthesis in the same way as all of the other eukaryotes.
choices.explanation: Not all eukaryotes have chloroplasts or cell walls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cells have a different genetic code from every other organism, and their DNA is not made of nucleotides.
choices.explanation: A shared ancestor would be reflected in shared molecular features.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cells have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles, and the DNA is organized into linear chromosomes.
choices.explanation: These are structural features that are expected in all eukaryotes.

explanation: All eukaryotes share membrane-bound organelles and linear chromosomes.

stem: Which finding would be most difficult to explain if all eukaryotes share a common ancestor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A eukaryote whose chromosomes are linear and are condensed with proteins during the division of the cell
choices.explanation: Linear chromosomes are a shared feature of eukaryotes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A eukaryote whose cells have a nucleus but whose chromosomes and genes are in no way similar to those of any other eukaryote
choices.explanation: A common ancestor predicts shared features such as linear chromosomes and genes with introns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A eukaryote whose cells have mitochondria that are surrounded by a double membrane like those of other eukaryotes
choices.explanation: Shared organelles are expected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A eukaryote whose genes contain introns that are similar to the introns in the genes of a distantly related eukaryote
choices.explanation: Shared introns are expected if there was a common ancestor.

explanation: Common ancestry predicts shared structural and genetic features.

stem: A hospital treats a bacterial infection with an antibiotic, and a few bacteria survive and multiply. Later infections in the hospital are resistant to the antibiotic. Which statement best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A few bacteria already had a mutation for resistance, and the antibiotic selected for them, so they reproduced and became common.
choices.explanation: Resistance to antibiotics evolves by selection of mutations that are already in the population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The antibiotic caused the bacteria to mutate in the way that they needed, so every bacterium became resistant to it in a single step.
choices.explanation: Mutations are random and are not directed by the antibiotic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each bacterium learned to resist the antibiotic during its life, and then passed on its learned resistance to its offspring.
choices.explanation: Acquired traits are not inherited in this way.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patient developed resistance to the antibiotic, and the resistance was passed to the bacteria that live in the body.
choices.explanation: Resistance is a property of the bacteria and not of the patient.

explanation: Antibiotic resistance evolves by natural selection.

stem: A farmer uses the same insecticide each year, and over several years it kills fewer and fewer insects. Which statement best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each insect becomes immune to the insecticide after it is sprayed once, and the immunity is passed on to its offspring.
choices.explanation: Individual insects do not acquire heritable immunity in this way.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The insects that are killed by the insecticide are replaced by insects of a different species that are better at finding food.
choices.explanation: The explanation is a change in the frequency of alleles within a species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insects with alleles for resistance survive and reproduce more than the others, so the frequency of the alleles rises in the population.
choices.explanation: Evolution of resistance to pesticides is an example of ongoing evolution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The insecticide becomes weaker as it is used more, because the chemicals in it break down faster in each year than they did in the year before.
choices.explanation: The explanation is in the evolution of the insects and not in the chemistry of the insecticide.

explanation: Resistance to pesticides evolves by natural selection.

stem: Influenza viruses change from year to year, so a new vaccine is needed in most years. Which statement best explains how the viruses change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The viruses decide which genes to change in order to be able to infect more people in the next year of the season.
choices.explanation: Viruses do not make decisions, and mutations are random.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mutations in the viral genome add variation, and variants that evade the immune responses of people are selected, so pathogens evolve.
choices.explanation: Pathogens evolve and cause emergent diseases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who are vaccinated pass the vaccine to the viruses, and the viruses use the vaccine in order to change their genes.
choices.explanation: Vaccines do not change the genes of viruses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The viruses never change from year to year, and so the new vaccines are made only to give people a chance to produce more antibodies each year.
choices.explanation: Viruses do change, and that is why the vaccines are updated.

explanation: Pathogens evolve, which can lead to emergent diseases.

stem: A tumor shrinks during chemotherapy, and then it regrows and no longer responds to the drug. Which statement is the most consistent with natural selection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cancer cells that survived stopped dividing completely, so the tumor grew back by a process other than cell division.
choices.explanation: Tumors regrow by the division of the cells that survive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A few cancer cells in the tumor were resistant to the drug, and they survived and divided, so the tumor cells became mostly resistant.
choices.explanation: Evolution of resistance to chemotherapy drugs is an example of ongoing evolution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All of the cancer cells in the tumor changed together to become resistant, because the drug told them to change their DNA.
choices.explanation: A drug does not direct mutations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The healthy cells of the patient became resistant to the drug, and so they could also take over the place of the tumor cells.
choices.explanation: The resistance is in the tumor cells that survive.

explanation: Cancer cells can evolve resistance to chemotherapy by selection.

stem: Which observation about the fossil record supports the claim that evolution is a continuing process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fossils from successive layers of rock show gradual changes in the traits of a lineage, and there is no point at which change stops.
choices.explanation: A continuous change in the fossil record is evidence that species have evolved and continue to evolve.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fossils are found only in the youngest layers of rock, and none of the older layers of rock contain any traces of organisms.
choices.explanation: Fossils are found in older layers too.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fossils of the same species are found in every layer of rock, and they have exactly the same traits in all of the layers.
choices.explanation: No change in the fossils would suggest that no evolution occurs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fossils of extinct species are found, but the traits of the living species are exactly the same as the traits of the extinct species.
choices.explanation: Different traits in living and extinct species suggest change over time.

explanation: A continuous change in the fossil record shows that evolution is ongoing.

stem: The graph shows the percent of infections caused by resistant bacteria in six regions that differ in their use of an antibiotic. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Regions in which the antibiotic is used more have more resistant bacteria, which is consistent with selection for resistance by the antibiotic.
choices.explanation: Resistant bacteria are favored when the antibiotic is used, so they become a larger percent of the infections.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The use of the antibiotic has no effect on the percent of resistant bacteria, because some resistant bacteria are found in every region.
choices.explanation: The percent rises with use, which shows an effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Using the antibiotic more often makes the bacteria in the infections mutate to become resistant, as the graph shows.
choices.explanation: The graph shows a correlation. It does not show that the antibiotic causes the mutations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regions in which the antibiotic is used less have more resistant bacteria, because the resistant bacteria are favored when no antibiotic is used.
choices.explanation: The percent of resistant bacteria is lower where there is less use of the antibiotic.

explanation: Antibiotic use selects for resistant bacteria.

diagram.altText: Percent of infections caused by resistant bacteria against antibiotic use. It rises from 2 percent at no use to 52 percent at 50 doses per 1,000 people per day.
diagram.xLabel: Antibiotic use (doses per 1,000 people per day)

stem: A scientist hypothesizes that the resistance of a weed to a herbicide came from alleles that were already in the population before the herbicide was used. Which investigation would best test this hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spray the herbicide on a single seedling of the weed and see whether the seedling survives for a week or more.
choices.explanation: A single plant is too small a sample, and the result would not show how common the alleles are.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grow seedlings of the weed in a greenhouse with no herbicide, and measure the height of all of the seedlings after a month.
choices.explanation: This does not test resistance to the herbicide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spray the herbicide on many seedlings from a population that has never been exposed to it, and see whether any of them survive.
choices.explanation: If some seedlings of an unexposed population survive, resistance alleles were present before exposure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spray the herbicide on many seedlings of the weed that have already been exposed to the herbicide for several years in the field.
choices.explanation: Previously exposed plants cannot show whether the alleles were there before exposure.

explanation: To test whether variation preexisted, expose a population with no history of exposure.

stem: Scientists sequence the genomes of a virus from patients in each of five years. The genomes from the later years differ from the genomes from the first year in more positions. Which statement is best supported by this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The genome of the virus cannot change, because the sequences from the five years must all be identical in order to be of one virus.
choices.explanation: Viral genomes accumulate mutations over time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The genome of the virus has changed over time, which is evidence that the virus is evolving.
choices.explanation: Genomic changes over time are an example of ongoing evolution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The patients changed the genome of the virus on purpose, because they chose the sequence that gave the best protection.
choices.explanation: Patients do not choose the genome of a virus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The virus has stopped evolving, because the differences are not equal in each of the five years that were studied.
choices.explanation: Differences that accumulate show evolution that is still occurring.

explanation: Genomic changes over time show that evolution is ongoing.

stem: What does a node (a branching point) on a phylogenetic tree or a cladogram represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The most recent common ancestor of the two groups or lineages that branch from it
choices.explanation: The nodes on a tree represent the most recent common ancestor of any two groups or lineages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The time at which all of the organisms on the tree died out and a new group of organisms began to form
choices.explanation: A node represents a split of a lineage and not an extinction of all of the organisms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The single trait that is most different between the two lineages that branch from it on the tree
choices.explanation: A node represents a common ancestor, and not a difference between the two lineages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The point at which one of the two lineages that branch from it changed into the other lineage in the tree
choices.explanation: A node is an ancestor of both lineages. One lineage did not change into the other.

explanation: A node is the most recent common ancestor of the lineages that branch from it.

stem: In a phylogenetic tree or cladogram, what does the outgroup represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lineage that has become extinct before any of the other organisms in the tree appeared, and that has no living relatives at all
choices.explanation: The outgroup is not necessarily extinct.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lineage that is least closely related to the other organisms in the tree, and that is used as a reference for the comparison
choices.explanation: The outgroup is the lineage that is least closely related to the remainder of the organisms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lineage that is most closely related to all of the other organisms in the tree, and that has the most derived traits
choices.explanation: The outgroup is the least closely related lineage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lineage that has the largest number of species in the tree, and that is located at the top of the diagram
choices.explanation: The outgroup is defined by how closely it is related, not by its number of species.

explanation: The outgroup is the lineage least closely related to the rest.

stem: The cladogram shows the relationships of six animals, with the numbered branching points. Which number represents the most recent common ancestor of the lizard, the mouse and the human?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1, because it is the oldest node that is shared by the lineages that have jaws, and so it includes all of the animals.
choices.explanation: Node 1 includes the shark and the salamander as well as the other three animals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 4, because the mouse and the human branch from each other at that node, which is the most recent branching point on the tree.
choices.explanation: Node 4 is the common ancestor of the mouse and the human only. It does not include the lizard.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 2, because it is the node at which the salamander branches off from the lineage that leads to the lizard, the mouse and the human.
choices.explanation: Node 2 is the common ancestor of the salamander, the lizard, the mouse and the human.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 3, because the lizard branches from the lineage that leads to the mouse and the human at that node, and no other node includes all three.
choices.explanation: Node 3 is where the lizard lineage splits from the lineage of the mouse and the human.

explanation: A node is the most recent common ancestor of the groups that branch from it.

diagram.altText: Cladogram of six animals. The lamprey branches off first. The shark branches next, after the trait jaws appears at node 1. The salamander branches next, after four limbs appears at node 2. The lizard branches next, after the amniotic egg appears at node 3. The mouse and the human share node 4, after hair appears.

stem: According to the cladogram, which trait is a shared derived character that supports a closer relationship between the mouse and the human than between either of them and the lizard?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jaws, because it was gained before the shark branched off, so it is found in most of the animals and does not separate them.
choices.explanation: Jaws are shared by five of the six animals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The amniotic egg, because it was gained before the lizard branched off, so the lizard has it too and it does not separate them.
choices.explanation: The amniotic egg is shared by the lizard, the mouse and the human.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four limbs, because it is a trait that the mouse and the human share, and the lizard does not have it in this tree.
choices.explanation: The lizard is placed after the trait four limbs was gained, so it has four limbs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hair, because it was gained in the lineage that leads to the mouse and the human, after the lizard had branched off.
choices.explanation: A trait that appears on the branch into node 4 is shared only by the mouse and the human.

explanation: Shared derived characters indicate common ancestry.

diagram.altText: Cladogram of six animals. The lamprey branches off first. The shark branches next, after the trait jaws appears at node 1. The salamander branches next, after four limbs appears at node 2. The lizard branches next, after the amniotic egg appears at node 3. The mouse and the human share node 4, after hair appears.

stem: Which statement correctly compares a phylogenetic tree with a cladogram?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A phylogenetic tree can show the amount of change over time, calibrated by fossils or a molecular clock, but a cladogram does not show time or the size of the differences.
choices.explanation: Trees show the amount of change over time, and cladograms do not show a time scale or the evolutionary differences between groups.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A phylogenetic tree and a cladogram are the same, because both of them show the exact dates at which each group of organisms first appeared.
choices.explanation: A cladogram does not show a time scale.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A cladogram can show the amount of change over time, calibrated by fossils or a molecular clock, but a phylogenetic tree does not show time.
choices.explanation: This reverses the two kinds of diagram.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A cladogram shows the evolutionary relationships of living organisms only, and a phylogenetic tree shows the relationships of fossil organisms only.
choices.explanation: Both kinds of diagram can include living and fossil organisms.

explanation: Phylogenetic trees can show time and the amount of change; cladograms do not.

stem: A phylogenetic tree built from the morphology of species conflicts with a tree built from DNA sequences of the same species. Which statement is the best evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both trees must be exactly correct, because all of the data that are used to build a tree have the same level of reliability.
choices.explanation: Molecular data are typically more reliable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tree built from the DNA sequences is typically more accurate and reliable, because similar body shapes can evolve separately.
choices.explanation: Molecular data typically provide more accurate and reliable evidence than morphological traits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither tree can be correct, because phylogenetic trees cannot be built from either the morphology or the DNA of the species.
choices.explanation: Both kinds of data are used to build trees.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tree built from the morphology is always more accurate, because body shape is a trait that is under direct natural selection.
choices.explanation: Selection can produce similar shapes in unrelated species, which makes morphology less reliable.

explanation: Molecular data are typically more reliable than morphology for building trees.

stem: The table shows three derived traits in an outgroup and in three species. Which statement about the relationships is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Species A and Species C share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either of them does with Species B, because they share trait 1.
choices.explanation: Trait 1 is shared by all three species and it is not informative about which pair is closer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Species A and Species B share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either of them does with Species C, because they share trait 1.
choices.explanation: Trait 1 is shared by all three species, so it does not separate A from B and C.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The outgroup is the most closely related to Species C, because the outgroup has none of the traits and so it is similar to Species C.
choices.explanation: The outgroup lacks the derived traits and is the least closely related to the other species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Species B and Species C share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either of them does with Species A, because they share trait 2.
choices.explanation: Trait 2 is a shared derived character of B and C only, which indicates a more recent common ancestor.

explanation: Shared derived characters group species into nested lineages.

diagram.caption: Derived traits in an outgroup and three species

stem: Use the cladogram to count how many of the four labeled traits were gained in the lineage that leads from the base of the tree to the human.

choices.label: A
choices.text: One, because the tree shows only the trait hair on the final branch to the human, and the other traits belong to other animals.
choices.explanation: The traits gained earlier on the path are also traits of the human.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Three, because the human has jaws, four limbs and hair, but the amniotic egg is a trait that is found only in the lizard.
choices.explanation: The amniotic egg is gained before the lizard branched off, and the human is on the same lineage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two, because the human shares hair with the mouse and four limbs with the salamander, and these are the only traits that it shares.
choices.explanation: The human has all of the traits that were gained on the path to it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Four, because jaws, four limbs, the amniotic egg and hair were gained one after the other on the branches that lead to the human.
choices.explanation: The path from the base to the human passes through the four labeled traits.

explanation: Traits gained along a lineage are inherited by every descendant on that lineage.

diagram.altText: Cladogram of six animals. The lamprey branches off first. The shark branches next, after the trait jaws appears at node 1. The salamander branches next, after four limbs appears at node 2. The lizard branches next, after the amniotic egg appears at node 3. The mouse and the human share node 4, after hair appears.

stem: Sequence data from a newly sequenced species show that a species that was placed in one branch of a cladogram is more closely related to a different branch. What should scientists do with the cladogram?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Discard all of the cladograms of all of the species, because one new result shows that no cladogram can be used.
choices.explanation: One revision does not invalidate the method.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the DNA sequence of the species, because the cladogram is correct and so the sequence data must be wrong.
choices.explanation: The data are the evidence, and the hypothesis is revised.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keep the cladogram without changing it, because a cladogram that has been published cannot be changed by new evidence.
choices.explanation: Cladograms are hypotheses that are revised with new evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Revise the cladogram to match the new evidence, because cladograms represent hypotheses that are constantly revised.
choices.explanation: Phylogenetic trees and cladograms represent hypotheses that are constantly being revised based on evidence.

explanation: Cladograms are hypotheses that are revised as evidence changes.

stem: According to the cladogram, why is the presence of four limbs not useful for deciding whether the mouse is more closely related to the human or to the lizard?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four limbs is a trait that was lost in the human, so it cannot tell us anything about the relationships of the three animals.
choices.explanation: The tree shows the trait as gained, not lost, on the path to the human.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four limbs is a trait of the salamander only, so it can be used only to separate the salamander from the other animals.
choices.explanation: The trait is also found in the lizard, the mouse and the human.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only the lizard has four limbs, so the trait is found in one animal and cannot be used to compare the three animals.
choices.explanation: The mouse and the human also have four limbs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All three animals have four limbs, which were gained in a common ancestor of the three, so the trait does not separate them.
choices.explanation: A trait that is shared by all of the lineages being compared is not informative for the grouping.

explanation: Shared derived characters must separate the groups being compared to be informative.

diagram.altText: Cladogram of six animals. The lamprey branches off first. The shark branches next, after the trait jaws appears at node 1. The salamander branches next, after four limbs appears at node 2. The lizard branches next, after the amniotic egg appears at node 3. The mouse and the human share node 4, after hair appears.

stem: According to the biological species concept, which statement defines a species of sexually reproducing organisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A group of organisms that can interbreed and exchange genetic information to produce viable and fertile offspring
choices.explanation: The biological species concept defines a species as a group capable of interbreeding to produce viable, fertile offspring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A group of organisms that can mate with each other to produce offspring, whether or not the offspring are fertile
choices.explanation: The offspring have to be viable and fertile.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A group of organisms that share the same ancestor, however distant, and that are found in the same part of the world
choices.explanation: The biological species concept is based on interbreeding and not on distant ancestry.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A group of organisms that look alike and that live in the same habitat, whether or not they are able to interbreed
choices.explanation: Similar appearance is not the criterion of the biological species concept.

explanation: The biological species concept: a group capable of producing viable, fertile offspring.

stem: A river changes its course and divides a population of mice into two groups that cannot cross the river. Over thousands of generations the two groups become different species. Which term describes this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Convergent evolution, because the two populations became more similar to each other as they adapted to different habitats.
choices.explanation: Convergent evolution involves unrelated populations that become more similar.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Punctuated equilibrium, because the two populations did not change at all during the thousands of generations that passed.
choices.explanation: Punctuated equilibrium describes the rate of change and not geographic separation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sympatric speciation, because the two populations were found in the same place and exchanged alleles when they diverged.
choices.explanation: In sympatric speciation, the populations overlap geographically. Here they were separated by the river.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Allopatric speciation, because the two populations were geographically isolated from each other when they first diverged.
choices.explanation: Allopatric speciation occurs in populations that are geographically isolated.

explanation: Allopatric speciation occurs in geographically isolated populations.

stem: In a single lake, a population of fish splits into two groups. One group feeds only near the surface and the other group feeds only at the bottom, and the two groups no longer mate with each other. Which term describes this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allopatric speciation, because the two groups are separated by a physical barrier and are in different places in the lake.
choices.explanation: There is no geographic barrier. The groups live in the same lake.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sympatric speciation, because the two groups diverge while living in the same area, without a geographic barrier between them.
choices.explanation: Sympatric speciation occurs in populations with geographic overlap.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The founder effect, because a few individuals left the lake and started a new population in another part of the world.
choices.explanation: The groups are in the same lake, and no new population was started elsewhere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Convergent evolution, because the two groups become more similar to each other as they feed in different parts of the same lake.
choices.explanation: The two groups become more different, not more similar.

explanation: Sympatric speciation occurs in populations with geographic overlap.

stem: Two closely related species of frogs live in the same pond. The males of one species call at a frequency that females of the other species do not respond to. Which statement describes this mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is not a mechanism of reproductive isolation, because the two species of frogs can still be found in the same pond.
choices.explanation: Behavioral differences can isolate species that live in the same place.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a post-zygotic mechanism, because the offspring of a mating between the two species do not survive or else are sterile.
choices.explanation: In this example mating does not happen, so it acts before a zygote forms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a pre-zygotic mechanism, because it prevents mating, so no zygote is formed, and it maintains reproductive isolation.
choices.explanation: Pre-zygotic mechanisms act before the formation of a zygote.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a mechanism that increases gene flow between the species, because the frogs share the same pond in all seasons.
choices.explanation: The mechanism prevents gene flow.

explanation: Pre-zygotic and post-zygotic mechanisms maintain reproductive isolation.

stem: A horse and a donkey can mate and produce a mule, but the mule is sterile. Which statement best describes what this shows about the horse and the donkey?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are the same species, because they can mate and produce offspring, and this is the only criterion for a species.
choices.explanation: The offspring must be viable and fertile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are separate species, because a post-zygotic mechanism, the sterility of the hybrid offspring, prevents gene flow between them.
choices.explanation: The offspring are not fertile, so the horse and the donkey do not exchange genes through them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are the same species, because the mule is healthy and alive and so it will be able to produce a lineage of mules.
choices.explanation: The mule is sterile and so it does not start a lineage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are separate species, because a pre-zygotic mechanism prevents the horse and the donkey from ever mating with each other in the wild.
choices.explanation: They do mate. The isolation acts after the zygote forms.

explanation: Sterile hybrids are a post-zygotic isolating mechanism.

stem: The fossil record of a lineage of snails shows almost no change for millions of years, followed by a short period in which new forms appear. Which term describes this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic drift, in which allele frequencies in a small population change because of chance events from one generation to the next.
choices.explanation: Genetic drift is a mechanism and not a pattern of change in the fossil record.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Punctuated equilibrium, in which evolution occurs rapidly after a long period of stasis.
choices.explanation: Punctuated equilibrium is when evolution occurs rapidly after a long period of stasis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gradualism, in which evolution occurs slowly and steadily over hundreds of thousands or millions of years.
choices.explanation: Gradualism would show steady change over the whole period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Convergent evolution, in which unrelated lineages become more similar because of similar selective pressures.
choices.explanation: The pattern describes the rate of change in one lineage.

explanation: Punctuated equilibrium: rapid change after a long period of stasis.

stem: When a volcano forms a new island, a single species of finch reaches it and, over time, produces several species that use different foods. Which term best describes this rapid formation of many species from one ancestor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Convergent evolution, which makes unrelated species look alike when they are subject to the same selective pressures.
choices.explanation: The species came from one ancestor and became different.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bottleneck effect, which reduces the genetic diversity of a population after a large part of the population has died.
choices.explanation: The finches radiated into new species. The bottleneck effect is about loss of diversity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adaptive radiation, which is divergent evolution that is especially rapid when new habitats become available to species.
choices.explanation: Speciation rates can be especially rapid during times of adaptive radiation as new habitats become available.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gene flow, which prevents separate populations from diverging into different species by moving alleles between them.
choices.explanation: Gene flow prevents divergence, which is the opposite of what happened.

explanation: Adaptive radiation is rapid divergent evolution when new habitats open up.

stem: Sharks (fish) and dolphins (mammals) have a similar streamlined body shape, though they are not closely related. Which statement best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dolphins changed into sharks over time, because the dolphins that lived in the sea had to change in order to be able to survive.
choices.explanation: One lineage did not change into the other.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two lineages were isolated from each other in different places, which caused the two to diverge from a shared body shape.
choices.explanation: That would describe divergence and not the evolution of a similar shape in unrelated lineages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sharks and dolphins inherited the body shape from a recent common ancestor, which was a streamlined animal that lived in water.
choices.explanation: They are not closely related, and the shape evolved separately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Similar selective pressures in the water produced similar adaptations in the two lineages, and so it is convergent evolution.
choices.explanation: Convergent evolution occurs when similar selective pressures result in similar adaptations in different species.

explanation: Convergent evolution: similar selective pressures produce similar adaptations in different lineages.

stem: Four populations of a plant were crossed in the laboratory. The table shows whether each cross produced offspring and whether the offspring were fertile. According to the biological species concept, which conclusion is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Populations 1 and 2 are the same species, because only their cross produced viable, fertile offspring.
choices.explanation: Only the cross of populations 1 and 2 gave viable, fertile offspring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All four populations are the same species, because they were all crossed in the same laboratory with the same methods.
choices.explanation: The result of a cross, and not the place where it is made, determines whether populations are the same species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Populations 1 and 4 are the same species, because they did not produce offspring, which shows that they are alike in every trait.
choices.explanation: No offspring means that the populations are reproductively isolated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Populations 1 and 3 are the same species, because their cross produced offspring, and that is the only criterion for a species.
choices.explanation: The offspring are sterile, so the populations are isolated post-zygotically.

explanation: The biological species concept requires viable, fertile offspring.

stem: Two populations of a fish were separated when a lake divided into two lakes. Many generations later the water levels rose and the lakes joined again. Which observation would show that the two populations had become separate species?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fish from the two populations no longer interbreed, or they produce offspring that are either not viable or not fertile.
choices.explanation: Reproductive isolation, with no gene flow between the populations, shows that speciation occurred.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fish from the two populations are the same size as each other, though they lived for generations in separate lakes.
choices.explanation: Size alone does not show whether the populations are reproductively isolated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fish from the two populations interbreed freely and produce fertile offspring, which are found in both of the original lakes.
choices.explanation: Free interbreeding with fertile offspring shows that they are still one species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fish from the two populations look different in color but they produce fertile offspring when they mate with each other.
choices.explanation: Differences in appearance do not make separate species if they interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

explanation: Speciation is shown by reproductive isolation.

stem: Why is a population with high genetic diversity better able to survive a change in its environment than a population with little genetic diversity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A diverse population has more individuals than a population with little diversity, so the environment affects fewer of them at one time.
choices.explanation: Diversity refers to the variation in alleles and not to the size of the population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A diverse population produces mutations in response to the new conditions, so the mutations always give the needed alleles.
choices.explanation: Mutations are random and are not produced in response to the conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each individual in a diverse population can change its alleles when the environment changes, so that all of them survive.
choices.explanation: Individuals do not change their alleles in response to the environment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is more likely to contain some individuals with alleles that allow them to survive and reproduce under the new conditions.
choices.explanation: Genetically diverse populations are more resilient because they are more likely to contain individuals that can withstand the environmental pressure.

explanation: Genetic diversity increases the chance that some individuals can withstand a change.

stem: A new fungal disease spreads through a population of trees. In a population with high genetic diversity, some trees survive, but in a population of genetically identical trees, all of the trees die. Which statement best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The trees in the identical population chose not to resist the fungus, because they had no differences from each other to choose from.
choices.explanation: Trees do not choose whether to resist a disease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The diverse population contained trees with alleles for resistance, but the identical trees all lacked these alleles and were all equally susceptible.
choices.explanation: Not all of the individuals in a diverse population are susceptible to a disease outbreak.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The diverse population made new alleles for resistance after it was exposed to the fungus, which the identical trees were not able to do.
choices.explanation: Alleles for resistance must already be present, because mutations are random.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The trees in the diverse population were exposed to less of the fungus, because diverse trees repel the fungus from their leaves.
choices.explanation: Diversity does not reduce the exposure of the trees to the fungus.

explanation: Not all individuals in a diverse population are susceptible to the same threat.

stem: An allele makes the fur of mice thicker. Thicker fur helps mice to survive in a cold climate but makes them overheat in a hot climate. Which statement best describes the allele?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is neutral in both climates, because the thickness of the fur has no effect on how well the mice are able to survive.
choices.explanation: The thickness of the fur does affect survival in each climate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is adaptive in the cold climate and deleterious in the hot climate, because the selective pressures on the mice differ between the climates.
choices.explanation: Alleles that are adaptive in one environment may be deleterious in another because of different selective pressures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is deleterious in both climates, because every allele that changes the fur of an animal reduces the fitness of the animal.
choices.explanation: The allele is favored in the cold climate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is adaptive in both climates, because an allele that is useful in one environment has to be useful in every environment.
choices.explanation: An allele can be useful in one environment and harmful in another.

explanation: Alleles that are adaptive in one environment may be deleterious in another.

stem: Population X has 12 different alleles of an immune gene, and population Y has 2 alleles of the same gene. A new pathogen appears in both populations. Which prediction is the most reasonable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Population Y is more likely to contain individuals that resist the pathogen, because it has fewer alleles to be affected by it.
choices.explanation: Fewer alleles mean a lower chance that one of them gives resistance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both populations are equally likely to resist the pathogen, because the number of alleles of a gene does not affect resistance.
choices.explanation: Diversity increases the chance of some resistance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither population can be affected by the pathogen, because pathogens do not attack the individuals that have an immune gene.
choices.explanation: Pathogens can affect individuals that have immune genes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Population X is more likely to contain individuals that resist the pathogen, so it is less likely to decline or become extinct.
choices.explanation: Species and populations with little genetic diversity are at risk of decline or extinction.

explanation: Low genetic diversity puts a population at risk.

stem: A fungus attacks fields of a crop. The table shows the percent of the plants that survived in fields planted with one variety and in fields planted with five varieties. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The number of varieties had no effect on the survival of the plants, because some plants survived in both kinds of fields.
choices.explanation: The survival was much higher in the diverse fields.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fields with a single variety were more resilient to the disease, because all of the plants in them had the same alleles and so were protected.
choices.explanation: The uniform fields had a much lower survival.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The diverse fields had fewer plants infected by the fungus, because the fungus cannot infect plants of different varieties.
choices.explanation: The data show survival and not infection, and a fungus can infect several varieties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fields with higher genetic diversity were more resilient to the disease, because they were more likely to contain plants that withstood it.
choices.explanation: Genetically diverse populations are more resilient to environmental perturbation.

explanation: Genetic diversity increases resilience to a threat.
