stem: A population of 50,000 genetically diverse plants includes 1% with an allele for resistance to a disease. All of the plants without the allele die, and a population of 50,000 genetically identical plants without the allele is exposed to the same disease. How many plants are expected to survive in each population?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 49,500 in the diverse population and none in the identical population, because most plants lack the allele.
choices.explanation: Only the plants with the allele survive, and that is 1% of the plants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 500 in the diverse population and none in the identical population, because only the diverse population contains the resistance allele.
choices.explanation: 50,000 x 0.01 = 500 plants have the allele, and the identical plants all lack it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: None in either population, because a disease that kills all of the plants without the allele will also kill the plants with it.
choices.explanation: The plants with the resistance allele are not killed by the disease.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 500 in each population, because the same number of plants are exposed to the disease in each of the two populations.
choices.explanation: The identical population does not contain the allele, so no plant in it survives.

explanation: Diversity can preserve alleles that allow some individuals to survive.

stem: A small population of an endangered species has very low genetic diversity. Conservation biologists move a few individuals from another population into it. Which statement best explains the likely benefit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new individuals add alleles to the population, which increases its diversity and its ability to respond to environmental changes.
choices.explanation: Gene flow adds alleles and increases genetic diversity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The new individuals reduce the genetic diversity of the population, which reduces the chance that all of the individuals are lost.
choices.explanation: Reduced diversity increases the risk of loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The new individuals increase the mutation rate of the population, so that the population can change quickly in response to a new threat.
choices.explanation: Adding individuals does not raise the mutation rate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new individuals remove the alleles that the population already has, so that the whole population is made of the best alleles.
choices.explanation: Moving individuals in adds alleles. It does not remove the existing ones.

explanation: Gene flow can increase genetic diversity and resilience.

stem: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago (bya), the environment was too hostile for life until about 3.9 bya, and the earliest fossil evidence of life is 3.5 billion years old. Which statement is best supported by this evidence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Life probably originated between about 3.9 and 3.5 bya, because it could not exist before the environment cooled and it had left fossils by 3.5 bya.
choices.explanation: Together, the evidence gives a plausible range of dates for the origin of life.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Life originated at the same time as Earth, about 4.6 bya, because life must have been present when the planet was formed.
choices.explanation: The environment was too hostile for life until about 3.9 bya.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Life cannot have originated on Earth, because the environment was hostile for the first 700 million years of its existence.
choices.explanation: The environment became suitable after about 3.9 bya.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Life originated about 1 billion years ago, because the oldest fossils must be younger than the age of the oldest rocks.
choices.explanation: The earliest fossil is 3.5 billion years old, which is much older than 1 billion years.

explanation: Geological evidence gives a plausible range of dates for the origin of life.

stem: The environment of Earth was too hostile for life until about 3.9 bya, and the earliest fossil evidence of life is 3.5 billion years old. What is the longest possible time, in years, between the end of the hostile period and the earliest fossils?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 3,500 million years, because the earliest fossils are 3.5 billion years old and so that is the time.
choices.explanation: 3.5 billion years is the age of the fossils and not the time between the two events.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 700 million years, because that is the time from the formation of Earth to the end of the hostile period.
choices.explanation: This is the length of the hostile period. The question asks about the time after it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 7,400 million years, because the two dates are added to find the total time for life to arise.
choices.explanation: The time between two dates is found by subtracting one from the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 400 million years, because 3.9 - 3.5 = 0.4 billion years.
choices.explanation: (3.9 - 3.5) billion years = 400 million years.

explanation: The time between two dates is the difference between them.

stem: Which statement describes the RNA world hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: RNA could have been the earliest genetic material, and it may have been able to replicate and to catalyze reactions before DNA and proteins were present.
choices.explanation: The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA could have been the earliest genetic material.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Proteins were the earliest genetic material, and they stored the information that was later copied into RNA and then into DNA.
choices.explanation: Proteins do not store hereditary information that can be copied by base pairing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: RNA was produced by the first cells from DNA, and the cells then used the RNA to build the other molecules that they needed.
choices.explanation: The hypothesis describes a time before cells, in which RNA was the genetic material.

choices.label: D
choices.text: DNA was the earliest genetic material, and RNA appeared later as a copy of the DNA that was used to make the first proteins.
choices.explanation: The hypothesis proposes that RNA came first.

explanation: The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA was the earliest genetic material.

stem: Which of the following is an assumption of the RNA world hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At some time genetic continuity was assured by the replication of RNA, and base pairing was necessary for that replication.
choices.explanation: The hypothesis assumes that RNA replication assured genetic continuity and that base pairing is necessary for replication.

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA was present at the start and carried the information that was used to make the first RNA molecules of the first cells.
choices.explanation: The hypothesis considers a time before DNA was the genetic material.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replication of the genetic material did not need the pairing of bases, because it was done by the random joining of nucleotides.
choices.explanation: Base pairing is assumed to be necessary for replication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genetically encoded proteins were the catalysts of the first reactions, and they were needed to copy the first genetic molecules.
choices.explanation: The hypothesis assumes that genetically encoded proteins were not involved as catalysts.

explanation: Assumptions: RNA replication, base pairing, and no genetically encoded protein catalysts.

stem: A scientist wants to test a prediction of the RNA world hypothesis in the laboratory. Which result would best support the hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A short DNA molecule is found that can catalyze the joining of amino acids into proteins, in the absence of any RNA.
choices.explanation: This would not show that RNA alone can replicate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A protein is found that can catalyze the joining of nucleotides to copy RNA molecules, but only when there is DNA present.
choices.explanation: The hypothesis assumes that proteins were not involved as catalysts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A short RNA molecule is found that cannot be copied or change in any way, and that stays unchanged for many years.
choices.explanation: An RNA that cannot replicate does not support the hypothesis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A short RNA molecule is found that can catalyze the joining of nucleotides to copy other RNA molecules, in the absence of any protein.
choices.explanation: If RNA can catalyze its own replication without protein, then genetically encoded proteins were not needed as catalysts.

explanation: Evidence that RNA can catalyze and replicate supports the RNA world hypothesis.

stem: Fossils of ancient mats of microorganisms that are 3.5 billion years old were found in rocks. What does this observation indicate about when life originated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Life originated no later than about 3.5 bya, because organisms were already present and left fossil evidence by that time.
choices.explanation: The earliest fossil evidence sets the latest date for the origin of life.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Life originated after 3.5 bya, because fossils are found only in the rocks that are younger than the time of the origin of life.
choices.explanation: A fossil that is 3.5 billion years old shows that life already existed then.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Life did not originate on Earth at all, because organisms that are as old as 3.5 billion years could not have left fossils.
choices.explanation: Fossils from 3.5 bya are evidence that life existed on Earth by then.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Life originated exactly 3.5 bya, because the age of the oldest fossils found is always the age at which life began.
choices.explanation: Life could have begun earlier than the oldest known fossils.

explanation: The earliest fossils give an upper limit for the date of the origin of life.

stem: Earth formed about 4.6 bya, and the earliest fossil evidence of life is 3.5 billion years old. About what percent of the history of Earth had passed before the time of the earliest fossils?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 76%, because 3.5 / 4.6 is the fraction of the history of Earth that had passed.
choices.explanation: 3.5 / 4.6 is the fraction of the history that came after the earliest fossils were formed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 318%, because the age of the fossils is divided by the time before they formed.
choices.explanation: That ratio is not a percent of the history of Earth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 24%, because 4.6 - 3.5 = 1.1 billion years, and 1.1 / 4.6 is about 0.24.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 110%, because the difference of 1.1 billion years is multiplied by 100.
choices.explanation: The difference must be divided by the age of Earth to give a fraction.

explanation: Percent = part / whole x 100.
